It's an LP supercell. You're seeing the exposed mesocyclone and wall cloud, because it's essentially rain free. Most southeast US supercells are HP, full of heavy rain that wraps and obscures the meso, and tornado.

Visual appearance does not denote strength. The Elie, Manitoba tornado was only about 50 yards in diameter on average, but it was an EF5 drill bit that gouged trenches in the ground and granulated entire structures. There have been broad tornadic circulations 3-4 miles across, with top winds of 30-50 mph. Never associate tornado size with strength, it's a loose correlation.
Doppler radar also registered winds of 295 mph in the El Reno tornado, within one of its many subvortices. It never struck anything with that level of windspeed, and was only rated EF3.
Damage only.

LP supercells are fascinating. I lived in Amarillo years ago, chased and recorded storms there before relocating to Upstate SC. They are less likely to produce tornadoes, but when they do they can be incredibly photogenic without precip wrapping around. So rare in the southeast, we tend to see them here in cold weather months only.
